strengths: Introduces a novel, well-motivated framing (Problem 2.1) for weight-diff interpretability that cleverly sidesteps the ground-truth problem by using synthetic constructions with known answers, enabling reliable quantitative evaluation.
The proposed DIT method is simple, clearly motivated via a commutativity argument (Eq. 3), and easy to understand/implement as a LoRA adapter trained via SFT on synthetic labeled weight diffs.

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation across two proof-of-concept tasks (hidden trigger-gated behaviors and distributed news knowledge summarization), multiple model families/sizes (Qwen3, Gemma3), and sensible black-box baselines (base question, 20 questions, with/without trigger 'roofline').

Interesting and non-trivial generalization results: DIT trained on rank-1 LoRAs generalizes to higher LoRA ranks and even (with some degradation) to full-parameter finetuning, and generalizes to OOD triggers (zero-width space) not seen during training.

Commendable scientific honesty in reporting negative/limiting results (Section 6): near-zero cross-behavior generalization, complete failure at trigger inversion, which strengthens the paper's credibility and usefulness for future research directions.
Extensive appendices with implementation details, prompts, and detailed score breakdowns support reproducibility.
Efficient parallel multi-LoRA training infrastructure (Appendix E) is a nice engineering contribution enabling training of tens of thousands of weight diffs.
weaknesses: The evaluation is fundamentally a 'proof-of-concept' on synthetic, narrow, single-question tasks (single hidden topic, single headline) that are far from realistic weight diffs encountered in practice; the paper's own Section 6.1 shows the method fails to generalize across behavior types, undermining claims of 'comprehensive' understanding.

The core method is essentially standard LoRA finetuning with synthetic data generation; the technical novelty over closely related work (e.g., Pan et al. 2024's Latent Interpretation Tuning, Betley et al. 2025) is somewhat incremental — extending an existing paradigm from activations to weight diffs.

Reliance on LLM-judges (o4-mini) for scoring similarity on a 5-point scale introduces potential bias/noise, and no human evaluation or inter-rater reliability check is reported to validate judge quality.

The paper focuses exclusively on a single fixed question at train/test time (explicitly stated limitation), which is a significant restriction relative to the more general Problem 2.1 formulation motivating the work; true comprehensiveness (arbitrary questions) is untested.

Baselines such as '20 Questions' are relatively weak/simple; more sophisticated black-box probing techniques (e.g., investigator agents cited in related work) are not compared against, potentially overstating DIT's advantage.

Scalability of the approach to realistic, complex, multi-faceted finetunes (e.g., real instruction-tuning datasets, multi-topic finetunes) is untested and left as future work, limiting practical significance for the stated motivating applications (backdoor/poisoning detection).

The mechanistic understanding of why DIT works is minimal (Section 6.3 is a very preliminary weight-visualization with limited insight), so the paper offers limited scientific explanation of the phenomenon it reports.
Code/data links in Appendix A appear to be blank/placeholder in the manuscript, raising reproducibility concerns.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated new task formulation (WEIGHTDIFFQA) with an elegant solution to interpretability's usual ground-truth problem, since synthetic weight diffs with known answers can be constructed by design.
The DIT method itself is simple, clearly motivated (including a nice derivation in Appendix E showing it falls out naturally from an end-to-end learning formulation), and easy to implement via LoRA.

Extensive empirical validation across five different base models (Qwen3 and Gemma3 at multiple scales) and two distinct proof-of-concept settings (hidden persona/trigger detection and news headline summarization).

Strong and diverse set of baselines, including black-box probing (base question, 20 questions, with/without trigger) and a fairly sophisticated LLM-agent baseline with a scaling-over-query-budget analysis, which convincingly shows DIT outperforms realistic black-box alternatives.

Multiple generalization studies (across LoRA ranks, to full-parameter finetunes, to out-of-distribution triggers) that meaningfully test whether the adapter learns a general mechanism rather than overfitting to superficial patterns.

Commendable scientific honesty: the paper explicitly reports negative results (no cross-behavior generalization, complete failure at trigger inversion) and discusses plausible explanations and implications for future work rather than hiding them.
Robustness check using an independent embedding-based similarity metric corroborates the LLM-judge-based results, increasing confidence that the findings are not an artifact of the judge.

Very thorough appendices (extensive prompts, hyperparameters, compute/cost accounting, additional scaling experiments on adapter rank and data size, and preliminary weight-diff visualizations) that aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The method is only demonstrated in narrow, somewhat toy proof-of-concept settings (single hidden topic behind a trigger, single latent headline); realistic finetunes/backdoors typically encode many entangled behaviors, and it's unclear how DIT would scale to this complexity.

Cross-behavior generalization is essentially nonexistent (Table 6.1), and the adapter completely fails at trigger inversion, which are significant limitations for the stated real-world motivating applications (data poisoning, backdoor/trojan detection).

The paper restricts evaluation to a single fixed question per setting at both train and test time, which is a much weaker test than the general WEIGHTDIFFQA task defined in Section 2 (arbitrary questions q); comprehensiveness as operationalized is not actually evaluated.

Most experiments use small-to-moderate rank LoRA weight diffs; full-parameter generalization results are mixed (degraded on Qwen3-4B) and full-parameter/higher-capacity finetuning realistic in practice is under-explored.

Reliance on synthetic data generated by LLMs (e.g., persona/topic construction via system prompts, gpt-4o-mini-generated news stories) may create idiosyncratic artifacts that do not reflect naturally occurring finetuning distributions or real backdoors, limiting external validity.
Code/data repository links in Appendix A appear to be placeholders (empty), raising reproducibility concerns for the current version of the manuscript.

Evaluation depends substantially on LLM-judges (o4-mini) for both baseline answer extraction and scoring, which, despite the embedding-based robustness check, could still introduce systematic biases favoring certain phrasings.

The overall contribution, while methodologically interesting, is explicitly framed as a preliminary proof-of-concept with the authors acknowledging that scaling and generalization remain open problems, tempering the claimed significance/impact for real-world interpretability use cases.
